The View from SomewherePart I · The idea

Chapter 2

The bookkeeping machine

Web edition. Figure 2.5 is live: you can set the gap on every road and choose another network.

Here is a small invented example. Four towns trade one good, and nobody knows the price level in any of them. What people do know is the price gap along five roads: a merchant who carried the good from town 1 to town 2 saw it rise by 0.30 in logs, a merchant on the road from 2 to 3 saw it rise by 0.20, and so on, one number per road. The question is what a single set of four price levels can say about five gaps, and what is left over when it has said all it can.

You know the regression that answers it. Town fixed effects, five observations, one dropped level. This chapter takes that regression apart and looks at the pieces, because the pieces are all we need for the rest of the book. There are two of them, they are orthogonal, and each has a name and a picture. One piece is what the towns’ price levels can produce: a gradient. The other is what no set of price levels can produce, and it lives on the loops of the road network. Counting the loops takes one line of arithmetic, and once you have counted them you know how many overidentifying restrictions the data carry before you have looked at a single number.

Nothing here is new, and I will say where it was known. What I want is for the picture to become automatic, because from Chapter 3 on we keep using it, and the sheaf language in later chapters is this picture with more decoration.

2.1Prices, gaps and the matrix between them

Take a network of V towns and E roads. Give each road a direction, from one end to the other. The direction is bookkeeping and nothing more: it says which way a gap is measured. Reverse a road and you flip the sign of its gap and nothing else changes. Figure 2.1 shows the four-town network of the opening, with roads 1→2, 2→3, 3→4, 4→1 and a diagonal 1→3.

A list of prices p=(p1,…,pV) lives in RV. A list of gaps t=(te)e∈E lives in RE; I will call RE edge space. The model is that each gap is a difference of prices, tu→v=pv−pu, and stacking the roads gives t=Dp with De,w={−1if road e leaves town w,+1if road e arrives at town w,0otherwise. That is the incidence matrix of the directed graph, one row per road and one column per town, and it is also what topologists call the coboundary: it takes something defined on points to something defined on connections. It is the design matrix of a Bradley–Terry model, of the worker–firm regression on a mobility network, of any model in which only differences are observed. Each row is the drawing read off one road, and each column is the drawing read off one town: the column for town w has a +1 on every road coming in and a −1 on every road going out. I will come back to the columns, because they turn out to be the cuts.

Turn the crank once. With p=(1,3,6,2) the gaps are Dp=(2,3,−4,−1,5). Go around the square 1→2→3→4→1 and add the gaps you meet, 2+3−4−1=0, as you must, since you return to the price you started at. Go around the top triangle 1→2→3 and back along the diagonal against its arrow, and you meet 2+3−5=0. Gaps that came from prices cancel around every loop. We are about to ask for the converse.

2.2Two subspaces of edge space

The matrix D maps RV into RE. Its image is the set of gap lists that some price list produces exactly. Call these the gradients, since Dp is the discrete gradient of the potential p. Two facts about it are all we need.

What D ignores. If Dp=0 then every road has the same price at both ends, so p is constant along every road, and therefore constant on every connected piece of the network. For a connected network the null space is the line spanned by 1=(1,…,1): add a constant to every price and no gap moves. This is the normalization you drop a fixed effect for. If the network has c connected pieces the null space has dimension c, one free level per piece, which is the connected-set logic of the worker–firm literature. Hence rankD=V−c.

What D cannot reach. The image of D is a subspace of RE of dimension V−c, which is smaller than E as soon as the network has more roads than a tree needs. Its orthogonal complement is the set of gap lists x with D⊤x=0. Read that condition through the columns of D. Column w of D is +1 on roads into w and −1 on roads out of w, so the w-th entry of D⊤x is the net amount arriving at town w: (D⊤x)w=∑e into wxe−∑e out of wxe. Setting that to zero says that every town’s books balance: whatever comes in goes out. A list x with this property is a circulation, and the simplest circulation is a number running once around a loop. In the four-town network the top triangle gives ℓ1=(+1,+1,0,0,−1)on roads (12,23,34,41,13),ℓ1=(+1,+1,0,0,−1)on roads (12,23,34,41,13), a unit going 1→2→3 and then back along the diagonal, which is the 13 road traversed against its arrow. The bottom triangle 1→3→4→1 gives ℓ2=(0,0,+1,+1,+1). Check town 3: its books receive ℓ1’s 23 flow and send out ℓ1’s 13 flow, and balance. Their loop sums against a gap list t are ℓ1⊤t=t12+t23−t13 and ℓ2⊤t=t34+t41+t13, and between them they give back the two restrictions we checked by hand above: the triangle is ℓ1 and the square is ℓ1+ℓ2.

The space of circulations is the cycle space, and it is the orthogonal complement of the gradients. Put the two together and edge space splits: RE=imD⏟gradients ⊕ ker⁡D⊤⏟loops. This is the fundamental theorem of linear algebra applied to D, and it is the whole chapter. Everything that follows is a consequence of it plus a count.

A picture in three dimensions. The smallest case where both pieces are non-trivial, with no two roads between the same pair of towns, is the triangle, with roads 1→2, 2→3, 3→1 and D the matrix with rows (−1,1,0), (0,−1,1), (1,0,−1). Its edge space is R3, and Figure 2.2 draws it. Gradients are the gap lists that sum to zero, which is the plane through the origin perpendicular to (1,1,1). The cycle space is the one remaining direction, the line along (1,1,1): one unit of circulation around the triangle, with every road carrying the same amount because every road points the same way around.

The picture is also an argument. Pick any t∈R3 and drop a perpendicular to the plane. The foot is a gap list that prices can explain, the dashed step is a circulation, and they are orthogonal. Nothing but the loop sum was needed to find the dashed step. For t=(0.30,0.20,−0.10) the loop sum is 0.40, and the dashed step puts a third of it on each road: (0.133,0.133,0.133). The foot is (0.167,0.067,−0.233), which is Dp⋆ for the potentials p⋆=(−0.133,0.033,0.100) with the level fixed by ∑p=0. The share of ∥t∥2=0.14 that the gradient accounts for is 1−0.0533/0.14=0.62.

2.3Counting loops without looking

The cycle space has dimension E−rankD. From rankD=V−c, dim⁡ker⁡D⊤=E−V+c. For a connected network, E−V+1. The triangle has 3−3+1=1 loop. The square with a diagonal has 5−4+1=2, matching the two triangles ℓ1,ℓ2 above. The big square 1→2→3→4→1 is a third loop that adds no restriction, because its loop vector is ℓ1+ℓ2 (the two diagonal terms cancel). The number counts independent restrictions, not cycles you could trace on the map.

A concrete basis makes the count visible. Choose a spanning tree: a set of V−1 roads that connects every town and closes no loop. Every road outside the tree closes exactly one loop with it, by going along the tree from one end to the other. Those fundamental loops number E−(V−1) and are independent, since each contains a road that no other fundamental loop contains. Figure 2.3 does this on ten towns. Take the ring of ten towns with five chords across it. A path through all ten towns is a spanning tree with nine roads. The tenth ring road and the five chords are outside the tree, so there are six independent loops, 15−10+1=6, and any further loop you trace is a combination of those six.

Network on ten towns Roads E rankD=V−1 Loops E−V+1 Loops per road
Path 9 9 0 0
Ring 10 9 1 0.10
Ring with 5 chords 15 9 6 0.40
Complete graph 45 9 36 0.80

On a tree there is nothing to test. A tree has E=V−1, so the cycle space is zero and the gradients fill all of edge space: any list of gaps at all is exactly some price list’s gradient. You may let the merchants make their numbers up and no arithmetic will catch them. This is the sentence the book keeps returning to: inconsistency can only live on a loop. Along a chain each town adjusts to the one before it and nobody at the far end objects. A contradiction needs a route by which the story can travel round and meet itself. The chain is just-identified, and every road you add beyond a tree buys one testable restriction.

2.4Cuts, the other side of the same space

The gradients have a second description, and it explains why a loop and a gradient can never overlap. Take any set S of towns and let 1S be the potential that is 1 on S and 0 elsewhere. Its gradient D1S is 0 on any road with both ends inside S or both outside, +1 on a road that arrives in S from outside and −1 on a road that leaves S. This is the cut defined by S: it lists the roads that cross the boundary of S, with a sign for which way. Because 1S is a sum of unit potentials, D1S is a sum of columns of D, and a sum of columns is in the image. So every cut is a gradient, and every gradient is a combination of cuts, since the columns of D are the cuts of single towns. The gradient space is the cut space.

Figure 2.4 takes S={1,4} in the four-town network. The roads 1→2, 1→3 and 3→4 cross; 4→1 is inside S and 2→3 is outside it. The cut is (−1,0,+1,0,−1) on roads (12,23,34,41,13).

Orthogonality is now a one-line fact. A circulation enters S exactly as often as it leaves, with the signs that make the net zero, so its dot product with any cut is zero. Cuts live in the image of D, loops live in the kernel of D⊤, and the two are perpendicular by the fundamental theorem. The count has a dual form, too: a spanning tree has V−1 roads and gives V−1 independent cuts, one per tree road, and the roads outside the tree give E−V+1 independent loops. The two numbers add to E.

2.5The split, and the regression you already run

Now the question the chapter opened with. Given any list of gaps t∈RE, the decomposition RE=imD⊕ker⁡D⊤ says that t=Dp⋆⏟gradient part+r⏟loop part,D⊤r=0,t=Dp⋆⏟gradient part+r⏟loop part,D⊤r=0, and the split exists and is unique, for any t, because a direct sum decomposes every vector in exactly one way. The potentials p⋆ are unique up to one constant per connected piece. To find them, apply D⊤ to both sides: D⊤t=D⊤Dp⋆, the normal equations. The matrix D⊤D is the graph Laplacian, with the number of roads at a town on its diagonal and −1 for each road between two towns. It is singular exactly in the constant directions, which is why you normalize. The vector D⊤t is the net arrival of reported gaps at each town: the books you would balance by hand if you treated the gaps as flows.

Figure 2.5 does this for the opening example. With gaps t=(0.30,0.20,0.10,−0.50,0.60) on roads (12,23,34,41,13), the two loop sums are ℓ1⊤t=0.30+0.20−0.60=−0.10,ℓ2⊤t=0.10−0.50+0.60=0.20.ℓ1⊤t=0.30+0.20−0.60=−0.10,ℓ2⊤t=0.10−0.50+0.60=0.20. The potentials with ∑p=0 are p⋆=(−0.35,−0.0375,0.175,0.2125). The gradient part Dp⋆ and the loop part r are in the figure. The loop part is small, ∥r∥2=0.01375 against ∥t∥2=0.75, so the gradient accounts for R2=0.98 of ∥t∥2. It also carries the loop sums exactly: r12+r23−r13=−0.0125−0.0125−0.075=−0.10, and r34+r41+r13=0.0625+0.0625+0.075=0.20, while the gradient part has zero loop sum on both. All of the going-round has ended up in r.

Now read the same object as econometrics. The model is t=Dp+ε, and p⋆ is the least-squares estimate under the normalization ∑p=0 (or any other one per connected piece). The gradient part Dp⋆ is the fitted value, and the loop part is the residual r=Mt with M=I−D(D⊤D)+D⊤ the residual maker. Three things follow that that are quick to prove and that the picture makes visible.

  • The fit does not depend on the normalization. Different normalizations change p⋆ by a constant on each piece and leave Dp⋆ alone. Fitted values are identified; levels are not.

  • The restrictions are the loops. Let B be any matrix whose rows span the cycle space, for instance the fundamental loops. Then BD=0, so Bt=Bε whatever the prices are. The hypothesis that a price system fits exactly is Bt=0, which is E−V+c linear restrictions on the data: the model is overidentified by exactly the number of independent loops, and the loop sums Bt are the moments you would test. The residual sum of squares ∥Mt∥2 is a quadratic form in them.

  • Errors enter only through the loop part of themselves. Since M annihilates D, Mt=Mε under the null, so the residual contains the noise’s projection onto the cycle space and nothing else. With ε∼N(0,σ2I) that is where a χ2 with E−V+c degrees of freedom comes from. Chapter 3 builds the test. If the errors have a known covariance other than σ2I, the same split holds in the inner product weighted by its inverse, and the two pieces are orthogonal in that metric instead.

The vocabulary of the topologists is a relabeling of what is on the page. The matrix D is the coboundary δ, what it ignores is H0, what it cannot reach is H1, and “t fits exactly” is “t is a coboundary”. Later chapters use these words. For now it is enough to know that H0 is the null space of D and H1 is the residual space, which has dimension E−V+c and which the inner product lets you identify with the cycle space.

2.6What the papers say

What the paper says: Jiang, Lim, Yao and Ye (2011), “Statistical ranking and combinatorial Hodge theory”

Of what we read, this is the closest published relative of the split in this chapter. They treat pairwise rankings as flows on the edges of a comparison graph and split every such flow orthogonally into a gradient flow, whose potential is the least-squares global ranking, and a divergence-free flow, which is a circulation in the sense above. They then split the circulations once more, into a curl part that measures inconsistency on triangles and a harmonic part that is inconsistency only on longer loops. We read the arXiv version’s introduction in full, every statement of a definition, lemma, theorem and proposition, the openings of Sections 2, 5 and 6, and the experiments and conclusion selectively, but not the proofs, Section 3 or most of Sections 4 and 7. In what we read, the paper gives no sampling distribution and no test for the loop part; it reports two descriptive ratios. It also says plainly that cyclic inconsistency may be an inherent property of the data, and not always noise to be removed. The curl and harmonic split goes beyond this chapter: it needs triangles to count as filled in, and it is a piece of their structure we have not used.

What the paper says: Hansen and Ghrist (2021), “Opinion dynamics on discourse sheaves”

They put one vector space on each node and each edge of a graph, with maps from node spaces to edge spaces, and call the resulting object a cellular sheaf. Put one number on every node and every edge and take the maps to be the identity, and, as we read it, the coboundary of the sheaf is the matrix D of this chapter and its sheaf Laplacian is D⊤D. Their H0 is the null space, the global sections, and they prove that opinion diffusion converges to the orthogonal projection of the starting opinions onto it. We read the paper in full except the proofs; what we read is stated for general vector spaces on nodes and edges, which is more than the constant case here; later chapters use the general case. There are no prices, noise or tests in it.

What the paper says: Baarda (1968) and geodetic reliability; Hill (1999)

We read these two only as summaries, and the claims below are leads rather than findings. Baarda’s reliability theory in geodesy gives each observation a redundancy number, these numbers sum to the network’s degrees of freedom, and observations are screened by normalized residuals; our “a tree cannot be tested” is the case where every redundancy is zero. Hill chains bilateral price comparisons along a spanning tree chosen to minimize a measure of spread, which makes the comparisons transitive by discarding every loop. In this chapter’s language: choosing a tree sets the obstruction to zero by throwing away its evidence. We did not find a geodesy text that states the zero-redundancy case explicitly, so that point is unverified.

What we did not read. The cycle space, the cut space and the count E−V+c are standard graph theory, and every statement in Sections 2.2 to 2.4 is a textbook fact that we argued here instead of citing. We read no graph-theory text for this project, so we give no page reference and make no claim about who stated what first.

2.7What we found

Cycle 1 was about the loop test, and its experiment is Chapter 3’s business. Three of its observations belong here, because they are about the count and not the test. In experiment 1 the networks were the four of the table above, all on ten towns, with σ=0.05 and 4000 replications per network. We computed the residual maker M=I−DD+ for each. Its diagonal entries are what Baarda calls redundancy numbers, and its trace equals the number of loops.

Network Loops Smallest Mee Largest Mee
Path 0 0 0
Ring 1 0.100 0.100
Ring with 5 chords 6 0.388 0.424
Complete 36 0.800 0.800

Three things came out of those numbers. First, the diagonal entries of M sum to E−V+1 in every network, which is the count above, confirmed numerically; we also checked trM=E−V+c and rankD=V−c on 500 seeded random graphs with 3 to 8 towns (seed 20261114) and found no mismatch. Second, on the ring every entry of M’s diagonal is exactly 1/10 and the residual is the loop sum divided equally among the roads, so a shift on any one road produces the same standardized residual on all ten. A test on the ring could see that something was inconsistent and could not say where: the hit rate for finding the shifted road was 0.092 against chance 0.10. In the ring with chords the same task succeeded 0.998 of the time against chance 0.067, and in the complete graph every time. Third, on a path every diagonal entry is zero, so nothing is checked at all. That is the tree, as a number.

Two caveats from the red-team pass belong with this. The loop test, the redundancy numbers and the localization rule were already known: the memo calls what we did a translation between geodesy, psychometrics, synchronization and Hodge ranking, which is useful as exposition, and not a research contribution. And the test needs the noise level σ from outside or from replicate reports on each road; one report per road cannot separate noise from a real loop sum. The earlier book’s chapter on the test presented it as though σ were simply available. Chapter 3 states what it takes to have it.

Try it

Try it 2.1. Seven towns are connected by eleven roads. How many independent loops are there? Now take a network of the same seven towns in two connected pieces, one of four towns with six roads and one of three towns with three roads. How many normalizations does it need, and how many independent loops does it have? Check that E−V+c agrees with the loops counted piece by piece.

Try it 2.2. On the four-town network of Figure 2.1, compute the cut of S={2} (the column of D for town 2). Take the dot product of that cut with ℓ1=(+1,+1,0,0,−1) and with ℓ2=(0,0,+1,+1,+1), and say in words why each comes out as it does.

Try it 2.3. For a ring of n towns with every road pointing the same way around, show that the loop part of any gap list t is (s/n)1 with s=∑ete. Conclude that Mee=1/n for every road, and say why a single road with an unusually large gap cannot be picked out from the ring alone. For the complete graph on n towns show that trM=(n−1)(n−2)/2, and check that the average diagonal entry is (n−2)/n, which is 0.8 for n=10.

Try it 2.4. In Figure 2.5, start on the four-town network with the chapter’s gaps and confirm its numbers. Switch to the path and watch the loop part stay at zero wherever you set the sliders. Switch to the ring and move one slider: every road’s loop part moves by the same amount. Then use the complete graph on four towns, choose gaps that sum to zero around every triangle, and watch the loop count of three stay put while the loop part vanishes.
